title: HL: Asymmetric information and market power (theory of the firm)
summary: HL only. When one side knows more than the other, markets fail through adverse selection and moral hazard. Firms’ costs, revenues and market structure determine output, price, profit and efficiency.

keyterms.definition: When one party in a transaction has more or better information than the other.
Asymmetric information before a transaction, e.g. sellers of used cars know their quality, so good products leave the market.
Asymmetric information after a transaction, when one party takes more risk because another bears the cost, e.g. insured drivers.
Ways to reduce information gaps: the less informed party gathers information (screening) or the informed party reveals it (signalling).
The minimum profit needed to keep a firm in the industry; total revenue just covers all economic costs including opportunity cost.
Profit above normal profit: total revenue exceeds total economic cost.
Firms maximise profit by producing where marginal cost equals marginal revenue (MC = MR).
Many small firms selling identical products, perfect information, free entry and exit; each firm is a price taker.
A single seller with high barriers to entry, facing the downward-sloping market demand curve.
Obstacles to new firms entering a market, e.g. economies of scale, legal protection, control of resources.
An industry where economies of scale are so large that one firm can supply the market at lower cost than several.
A market dominated by a few large interdependent firms, with high barriers to entry.
Agreement between firms to limit competition, e.g. fixing prices; formal collusion is a cartel.
Analysis of strategic decisions where each firm’s best choice depends on what rivals do, e.g. the prisoner’s dilemma.
Many firms selling differentiated products with free entry, so each has a little price-setting power.
The combined market share of the largest firms, e.g. a 4-firm ratio of 80% suggests oligopoly.

questions.prompt: A buyer of a used car cannot tell whether it is reliable, so she will pay only an average price. Good cars are withdrawn from sale. This is…
questions.explanation: Information asymmetry before the deal drives high-quality goods out of the market.

questions.statement: Moral hazard occurs when a party changes behaviour after a deal because someone else bears the risk.
questions.explanation: E.g. a bank taking big risks expecting a government bailout.

questions.text: Asymmetric information before a transaction leads to adverse ___.
questions.explanation: Adverse selection is a pre-contract problem; moral hazard is post-contract.

questions.prompt: Match each example to the concept.

pairs.left: Only the sickest buy health insurance

questions.explanation: Screening and signalling are responses; moral hazard and adverse selection are the problems.

questions.prompt: Which government response reduces asymmetric information in the market for doctors?
questions.explanation: Licensing and regulation guarantee minimum standards consumers cannot check.

questions.statement: Warranties offered by sellers can help solve adverse selection.
questions.explanation: They signal confidence in quality and shift risk to the seller.

questions.prompt: Why might health insurance premiums rise if insurance is voluntary?
options: Healthier people opt out, leaving a riskier pool of buyers
questions.explanation: Adverse selection: buyers know their own risk better than insurers.

questions.text: A bank expecting to be rescued may take more risk; this is moral ___.
questions.explanation: Moral hazard was a key issue in the 2008 financial crisis.

questions.prompt: Which is the best example of asymmetric information?
options: Both buyer and seller know the price of milk
A mechanic knows more than the customer about what repairs are needed
questions.explanation: The seller can exploit superior knowledge.

items: Sellers know quality; buyers do not
Owners of good cars withdraw them
Average quality and price fall further
questions.explanation: Adverse selection can shrink or destroy a market.

lessons.title: Costs, revenue, profit and perfect competition

questions.explanation: If MR > MC, an extra unit adds to profit; if MC > MR, it reduces it.

questions.statement: Normal profit is included in a firm’s economic costs.
questions.explanation: It is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur, so zero economic profit = normal profit.

questions.prompt: A firm sells 500 units at $12. Its average total cost is $10. What is its economic profit?
questions.explanation: TR = 6000, TC = 5000, so profit = $1000 above normal profit.

questions.text: In perfect competition each firm is a price ___.
questions.explanation: Each firm is too small to affect the market price, so its demand curve is horizontal at P = AR = MR.

questions.prompt: Why do perfectly competitive firms earn only normal profit in the long run?
options: Abnormal profits attract new entrants, shifting supply right until price = minimum AC
questions.explanation: Free entry and exit compete away abnormal profits and losses.

questions.statement: In the long run, a perfectly competitive firm is both allocatively (P = MC) and productively (min AC) efficient.
questions.explanation: It produces at the bottom of its AC curve and price equals marginal cost.

questions.prompt: Match each cost or revenue to its definition.

pairs.right: Extra cost of one more unit
Extra revenue from one more unit

questions.explanation: For a price taker, P = AR = MR.

questions.text: Profit above normal profit is called ___ profit.
questions.explanation: Also called supernormal or economic profit.

questions.prompt: Total revenue is $800 and total costs (including normal profit) are $900. The firm…
questions.explanation: TR < TC means an economic loss.

questions.prompt: Order the long-run adjustment in perfect competition after demand rises.
items: Price falls back until normal profit is earned
questions.explanation: Entry restores long-run equilibrium at minimum AC.

questions.prompt: Why is a monopoly allocatively inefficient?
options: It sets price above marginal cost and restricts output
questions.explanation: P > MC means society values extra units more than they cost, giving a welfare loss.

questions.statement: A natural monopoly arises because economies of scale let one firm supply the whole market at lowest cost.
questions.explanation: E.g. water pipes or power grids; duplicating the network would waste resources.

questions.prompt: Match each market structure to a feature.
questions.explanation: Number of firms, product type and barriers distinguish the structures.

questions.text: The top four firms in a market have shares of 30%, 25%, 15% and 10%. The 4-firm concentration ratio is ___%.
questions.explanation: 30 + 25 + 15 + 10 = 80%, indicating oligopoly.

questions.prompt: In the prisoner’s dilemma, why do two oligopolists often both cut prices?
options: They have perfect information about each other’s costs
Each fears the other will cheat, so cutting is the dominant strategy, though both would earn more by colluding
questions.explanation: Individually rational choices lead to a worse joint outcome.

questions.statement: A cartel is an example of formal collusion and is illegal in most countries.
questions.explanation: Competition law bans price fixing because it harms consumers.

questions.prompt: Why do firms in monopolistic competition earn only normal profit in the long run?
options: Free entry of firms with similar products reduces each firm’s demand
questions.explanation: New entrants take customers until AR is tangent to AC.

questions.text: Obstacles such as patents and economies of scale that keep new firms out are barriers to ___.
questions.explanation: High barriers let monopolies keep abnormal profit in the long run.

questions.prompt: Which is a possible benefit of monopoly?
options: Lower prices than perfect competition always
Abnormal profits can fund research and development
questions.explanation: Dynamic efficiency and economies of scale may offset some costs of market power.

questions.prompt: Order how a regulator might deal with a natural monopoly.
items: Identify a market with huge economies of scale
Allow a single supplier rather than many
Set a price cap or regulate prices
questions.explanation: Regulation aims to keep cost advantages while limiting abuse of market power.
